Read this before the number: this score explains what pushed gold's price today — it's built from how oil, interest rates and the dollar moved today. We also tested whether it can predict where gold goes over the next 1–20 trading days, and it can't — it has no real track record for that (see “Does the score predict what happens next?” on the reasoning page). Use it to understand today's move, not to guess tomorrow's. A big red number here is not a sell signal — if you're looking for tactical entry/exit timing, that's the separate “buy the dip, sell the high” panel below, not this one.
Today's readings

Silver's live price here is a same-day snapshot, but its full history is now charted below alongside gold and the miners — sourced from COMEX silver futures and rescaled to match this spot quote. (An earlier version of this dashboard said no free silver history existed; that turned out to be wrong, and it has been added.) Rates and oil come from the Federal Reserve’s FRED database, which publishes a day or more behind — any reading marked as of a date is that source’s latest real print, not today’s. Oil is shown as futures prices (current to the day); the scores and backtests use the FRED spot series instead, which lags days behind, and FRED’s Brent is the physical “Dated Brent” price, which can sit far above the futures price when supply is tight. The dollar is the ICE US Dollar Index (DXY); the scores themselves use the Fed’s broad trade-weighted index, which has the long history the backtests need.

Core Factor Score — the leaner, tracked score

Instead of all seven factors, use only the ones that actually move gold the most, weighted by that magnitude — then track every reading against what gold actually did afterward, so the score's real-world reliability can be checked directly rather than assumed.

Score calibration — when a score said “strong”, what did gold do next?

Every day since 2006 is put into a bucket by its score, then we look at gold's average return over the following 5, 20 or 60 trading days. If a score worked, the bars would climb from left (headwind) to right (tailwind), and sit clearly above or below the dashed line, which is what gold did on an average day.

Do the four scores agree — and does agreement mean anything?

When all four scores point the same way, it feels more convincing than when they split. Here that feeling is tested: every day since 2006 is labelled “all four tailwind”, “all four headwind”, “all four neutral” or “they disagree”, then we look at what gold did next.

Real yields vs gold — does the link change with the interest-rate regime?

Falling real yields (the bond rate after inflation) have usually helped gold. But how strongly gold reacts depends on where real yields already are. Each day is sorted by the previous day's real-yield level, so nothing looks ahead.

Volatility context — is today's move big or normal?

The same 1.5% gold move means something different in a calm market than in a wild one. Two measures: GVZ, the market's own forecast of gold volatility (from options), and realized volatility, how much gold actually moved over the last 20 days.

Gold held by the biggest gold ETF (GLD)

Real tonnes of gold in the SPDR Gold Trust, published daily by its sponsor. When investors buy the fund it must buy gold; when they sell, it releases gold. So this is a true flow measure, unlike the trading-volume figure elsewhere on this page.

Central-bank gold buying is the other big real-world driver, but no free source with automatic daily or monthly updates could be found (the World Gold Council's data needs a manual registration), so it is left out rather than typed in by hand.

Gold in rupees and euros

Gold is priced in dollars, but you may earn and spend in something else. The same ounce can rise faster or slower in another currency, because the currency itself moves against the dollar.

Built for tactical entry/exit timing; kept separate from the macro-causality analysis on the rest of this page.

How crowded is the gold trade right now?

Everything above is macro — rates, the dollar, oil: things that move gold but aren't about gold. This is the opposite: what traders are actually doing. Every week the CFTC publishes how heavily speculators are positioned long or short COMEX gold futures. The classic reading is contrarian — when almost everyone is already long, the marginal buyer is scarce. We tested whether that actually pays; the answer is below.

Gold vs. silver vs. the miners

All three rebased to 100 at the start of the window, so the lines show relative performance rather than price. Silver and gold miners are the two most common ways of taking a leveraged view on the same underlying trade — miners especially, since their profits move on gold's price minus a largely fixed cost base.

Time machine — what would this dashboard have told you?

Pick any past date and see the reading this dashboard would have shown that day, using only what was knowable then — then see what gold actually did next. This is the honest way to judge a signal: not by how it looks in hindsight, but by whether its past calls held up.

What's actually driving the score

How closely each factor's daily moves have actually tracked gold's price, over the last 4 years. The longer the bar, the more that factor matters to the score. Blue means it moves the same direction as gold; red means the opposite direction. A short bar means that factor barely matters — no matter how much attention it gets in the news.

Has gold's relationship with oil, the dollar and rates been changing?

The bars above are one average over 4 years — but relationships aren't always steady. This tracks how closely each factor has moved with gold within a rolling ~4.5-month window, so you can see a link strengthening, weakening, or even flipping direction. A line near 0 means barely any relationship right then; near ±1 means a very tight one.

What if...? (a historical rule of thumb, not a forecast)

Pick a factor and a hypothetical move, and see how much gold has typically moved on that same day, based on 4 years of actual data. This is a backward-looking sensitivity check — a way to build intuition for how tightly two things have moved together — not a prediction of what gold will do next (remember: the score has no proven ability to call tomorrow's move).

→ —

What if...? Which score zone would a day like this land in?

Enter a hypothetical one-day move for any factors and see where all four scores would land. The scores measure each day’s moves against the last 60 days’ typical moves, so a move that has been normal lately scores near neutral, and only an unusually large one pushes a score toward the extremes. Leave a factor at 0 for “no move”. Nothing here forecasts gold: it shows how the scores respond, and the scores have no proven forecasting power (see the calibration section above).

Compare two dates

Pick any two dates since 2006 and see what changed across every input and all four scores. Dates without a trading day snap to the nearest one.

Rates, oil and the Fed dollar index are forward-filled on days their source has not published, so a comparison that touches the most recent days can understate real changes there. Scores are the day’s own scores as rebuilt today.
